sentences.text: The Encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism On-Line, EROL in the census record, states its holding in its own heading as "INFORMATION ON AND PRIMARY DOCUMENTS FROM ANTI-REVISIONIST MOVEMENTS, ORGANIZATIONS AND PARTIES BY COUNTRY" (contents page), and the maryleelabor census enters it as an "online encyclopedia of information on, and primary documents from, anti-revisionist movements, organizations and parties, by country" (maryleelabor census record).

Harvard's Digital Handbook for Research on Soviet History catalogues it as a "Digital encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism developed by the Marxists Internet Archive, containing English translations of representative anti-Revisionist materials from China, Albania, and many western countries", in the format "Digital archive", item OARRSH_00098 of its Open Access Primary Sources (Harvard Digital Handbook).

It is entered from the Marxists Internet Archive's History section, "MIA: History: Encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism On-Line" (entry page), its contents page ends "Contact EROL Administrator" (contents page), and Harvard's record gives the Marxists Internet Archive as its creator and its parent source (Harvard Digital Handbook).

The census record has it held by "an EROL Administrator, under the Marxists Internet Archive", with "terms are not stated on the saved EROL pages", and records it as part of that archive by its URL, the relation unstated in prose on the contents page (maryleelabor census record).
Its definition page closes on its purpose: "The goal of the Encyclopedia of Anti-Revisionism is to document this trend", signed "Paul C., 2009" (What is Anti-Revisionism).

The trend, on the same page, is first the term's older use, "opposition to attempts to revise, modify or abandon the fundamentals of revolutionary theory and practice in a manner that was perceived to represent concessions to Communism’s adversaries", and in its specific meaning "a trend that developed in the pro-Soviet (as opposed to the Trotskyist) Communist movement after World War II" (What is Anti-Revisionism, Paul C., 2009).

It grew at the shift from wartime collaboration to the Cold War and at the crisis of the CPSU's 20th Congress in 1956, criticized the official Communist Parties "from the left" for abandoning orthodox Marxism-Leninism and for being insufficiently revolutionary, and made the defence of Stalin its hallmark once those parties joined Khrushchev's denunciation of him (What is Anti-Revisionism).

It expanded to communists aligned with Chinese or Albanian positions, reached its greatest size with Marxist-Leninist and Maoist parties after the Sino-Soviet split, grew with the Cultural Revolution and declined after Mao's death and the defeat of the Gang of Four, when some "soldiered on" and others argued for a non-Trotskyist "left-wing" communism independent of foreign authorities or models (What is Anti-Revisionism); the census record adds that "The tendency it records is itself a minority defined against 'revisionism'" (maryleelabor census record).

Its contents open with background, "A Brief definition of Anti-Revisionism" and representative materials from China and from Albania, and file the United States by three waves of anti-revisionism from 1946 to 1970 and by the New Communist Movement from its origins in 1969 through its party-building campaigns to 1977 (contents page).

The New Communist Movement sections that follow are titled "Birth of the Anti-Dogmatist Trend, 1976-1977", "Crises, Splits and More New Parties, 1977-1980", "Anti-Dogmatists Unable to Unite, 1978-1980", "Collapse and Aftermath" and "Major Issues and Debates", with an alphabetical index to all its subsections (contents page).

Canada runs from a post-war antecedent, Fergus McKean, to "Crisis and Collapse, 1982-1983", the United Kingdom from post-war antecedents through "High Tide: The Consolidation of Maoism by the Late 1970’s" to "Ebbing Tide: Decline and Dissolution", and 23 further countries from Australia to Switzerland have a section each (contents page), 26 country sections by the census's count, document counts not stated (maryleelabor census record).

The census record takes as its unit "a primary document of an anti-revisionist movement, organization or party, filed by country and by period subsection; periodicals listed by country", and as what it records 26 countries with China and Albania, the United States from 1946 to the New Communist Movement's collapse, Canada 1964 to 1983 and the United Kingdom to "decline and dissolution" (maryleelabor census record).

Its losing side, in the census record, is its structure: "the encyclopedia is organized around splits and defeat", shown by the United States, Canadian and British section titles (maryleelabor census record).

Its periodicals page lists the movements' papers and journals by country, among them The African World, Challenge/Desafio, the Progressive Labor Party's newspaper, Revolutionary Worker and Workers’ Advocate (1969-93) in the United States, The Forge and In Struggle in Canada and Proletarian in Britain (periodicals page), the list the census record counts among its holdings (maryleelabor census record).

It names periodicals by the splits that made them: the Chicago Workers’ Voice of "former members of the Marxist-Leninist Party", and the Young Communist "after it went with the Revolutionary Workers Headquarters in the RCP split" (periodicals page).

Its list runs past 1983, to Eureka (2000-2005), Demarcations ("starting in 2009") and The Line of March ("begun 2011") (periodicals page), where the census record gives the period from 1946 "to the 1980s", records movements that "ended or dissolved by its own section titles" and tags it "NOT a living movement's site" (maryleelabor census record).

The host gives itself as "an all-volunteer, non-profit public library, established in its present form in 1998", with 76 active volunteers in July 2025, bound by the tenets "We will always remain politically independent", "We do not ‘judge’ writers" and "Our priority is to provide archival information", endorsing none of the views of the writers it archives (MIA introduction, last updated 21 April 2026).

Its licence is the host's, "All material within these Archives, unless noted otherwise, is public domain" (MIA introduction), which the census record carries for EROL beside "not stated on the saved EROL pages", with access by "free public web pages" (maryleelabor census record); the Wikipedia article on the host says its collection is maintained by volunteers and its material free of charge, "although not necessarily free of copyright" (Wikipedia).

Harvard's record dates its materials "1946-1983", lists 26 places of coverage from the USSR, China and Albania to Switzerland, without India, Iran or the Philippines, and gives its subjects as anti-Revisionism, the Sino-Soviet split, foreign relations, the Cold War and ideology, its language English (Harvard Digital Handbook).

The same record states a limit: "This online resource has not been found to meet all criteria for legitimacy", for it "may reproduce copyright-protected content without license or permissions, contain re-typed content that cannot be verified for accuracy or completeness, and/or omit facts of publication or archival attribution" (Harvard Digital Handbook).

The census record states no limits of the saved pages ("not stated on the saved pages"), notes that the gathering method "is not described on the saved page", does not answer "the completeness of its holdings for any organization" or "the record of tendencies outside anti-revisionism", and leaves unchecked "who the EROL Administrator is, and how documents were gathered", its introduction page having returned HTTP 404 (maryleelabor census record).

The census asks of it "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", files it under movement documents, an area whose definition includes "the record of splits", and the texts of the tradition, with movement documents, periodical runs and primary texts as its evidence, and answers that it keeps "the anti-revisionist movements, organizations and parties: their primary documents and periodicals, in the encyclopedia's own periodization", which tells "how the encyclopedia periodizes a national movement's waves, splits and collapse" (maryleelabor census record).

The archive's reading in the record is "An organ that keeps a defeated tendency's record in that tendency's own documents, sectioned by its splits and its collapse, so each faction of a split stays stated after the organization that housed it ended"; it reads the "Anti-Dogmatists Unable to Unite" and "Major Issues and Debates" sections "as the losing side of the losing side kept for later readers, held by an archive independent of every party it records", and tags it "NOT an organ of any party it records" (maryleelabor census record).

The census names #1725, Ils ne sont pas marxistes, as its anchor (maryleelabor census record); #1725 holds that "Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender", and that otherwise "the defeated critique loses its organ, its holder and its route, and so cannot be taken up later" (#1725).

#1725 states the conventional reading first, in which "the New Communist Movement's succession of parties" looks like proof and "the left's problem is temperamental: too much fighting", and reads the record by its endings: "Disagreement is constant. What varies is the ending", a critique being "settled by vote, verdict or decree, with the losing position carried into nothing that follows" or leaving "with the people who hold it" (#1725).

Where a dispute concerns the group's identity, #1725 holds, "a split is the honest outcome, and the question becomes whether the split is recorded and argued or simply enacted", and where a critique was later taken up its critics "had a base and form of their own, a caucus, collective, journal or paper" (#1725).

#1725 draws its SDS case from a document in EROL's New Communist Movement section, the REP collective's account of the 1969 expulsion of Progressive Labor, calls the SDS record "the clearest single instance, because the winning side wrote it down", and concludes "The split took the place of the discussion" (#1725); Challenge/Desafio, the newspaper of the party expelled, stands on the encyclopedia's periodicals page (periodicals page).

The English Wikipedia has no article on it: the name redirects to "Marxists Internet Archive", whose article defines the host as "a non-profit online encyclopedia, created in 1990" and names its historical sections and a reference section, the "Encyclopedia of Marxism", without naming EROL (Wikipedia), which the census record tags "NOT a general encyclopedia of Marxism" (maryleelabor census record).

At its name the Overview carries the encyclopedia's "Definition, period, countries and periodicals", "Faithful to the encyclopedia's subject and range", with "The MIA named as its host", at a new address, the census name, for an external resource entered in the census the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

The Capture Registry records "THE SPLITS NOT CARRIED", "The composition gives the movement as a country entry", and "its periodization by splits, unity attempts and collapse, is not in the composition", and attributes to #1725 a reading of "EROL as a record kept of a movement's failure to hold its own critiques, organized by that failure" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31); #1725 names omission "the expulsion form: the contested record never reaches the answer-forming context" (#1725).

It expanded to communists aligned with Chinese or Albanian positions, reached its greatest size with Marxist-Leninist and Maoist parties after the Sino-Soviet split, grew with the Cultural Revolution and declined after Mao's death and the defeat of the Gang of Four, when some "soldiered on" and others argued for a non-Trotskyist "left-wing" communism independent of foreign authorities or models (What is Anti-Revisionism); the census record adds that "The tendency it records is itself a minority defined against 'revisionism'" (maryleelabor census record). Its contents open with background, "A Brief definition of Anti-Revisionism" and representative materials from China and from Albania, and file the United States by three waves of anti-revisionism from 1946 to 1970 and by the New Communist Movement from its origins in 1969 through its party-building campaigns to 1977 (contents page). The New Communist Movement sections that follow are titled "Birth of the Anti-Dogmatist Trend, 1976-1977", "Crises, Splits and More New Parties, 1977-1980", "Anti-Dogmatists Unable to Unite, 1978-1980", "Collapse and Aftermath" and "Major Issues and Debates", with an alphabetical index to all its subsections (contents page). Canada runs from a post-war antecedent, Fergus McKean, to "Crisis and Collapse, 1982-1983", the United Kingdom from post-war antecedents through "High Tide: The Consolidation of Maoism by the Late 1970’s" to "Ebbing Tide: Decline and Dissolution", and 23 further countries from Australia to Switzerland have a section each (contents page), 26 country sections by the census's count, document counts not stated (maryleelabor census record). The census record takes as its unit "a primary document of an anti-revisionist movement, organization or party, filed by country and by period subsection; periodicals listed by country", and as what it records 26 countries with China and Albania, the United States from 1946 to the New Communist Movement's collapse, Canada 1964 to 1983 and the United Kingdom to "decline and dissolution" (maryleelabor census record). Its losing side, in the census record, is its structure: "the encyclopedia is organized around splits and defeat", shown by the United States, Canadian and British section titles (maryleelabor census record). Its periodicals page lists the movements' papers and journals by country, among them The African World, Challenge/Desafio, the Progressive Labor Party's newspaper, Revolutionary Worker and Workers’ Advocate (1969-93) in the United States, The Forge and In Struggle in Canada and Proletarian in Britain (periodicals page), the list the census record counts among its holdings (maryleelabor census record). It names periodicals by the splits that made them: the Chicago Workers’ Voice of "former members of the Marxist-Leninist Party", and the Young Communist "after it went with the Revolutionary Workers Headquarters in the RCP split" (periodicals page). Its list runs past 1983, to Eureka (2000-2005), Demarcations ("starting in 2009") and The Line of March ("begun 2011") (periodicals page), where the census record gives the period from 1946 "to the 1980s", records movements that "ended or dissolved by its own section titles" and tags it "NOT a living movement's site" (maryleelabor census record). The host gives itself as "an all-volunteer, non-profit public library, established in its present form in 1998", with 76 active volunteers in July 2025, bound by the tenets "We will always remain politically independent", "We do not ‘judge’ writers" and "Our priority is to provide archival information", endorsing none of the views of the writers it archives (MIA introduction, last updated 21 April 2026). Its licence is the host's, "All material within these Archives, unless noted otherwise, is public domain" (MIA introduction), which the census record carries for EROL beside "not stated on the saved EROL pages", with access by "free public web pages" (maryleelabor census record); the Wikipedia article on the host says its collection is maintained by volunteers and its material free of charge, "although not necessarily free of copyright" (Wikipedia). Harvard's record dates its materials "1946-1983", lists 26 places of coverage from the USSR, China and Albania to Switzerland, without India, Iran or the Philippines, and gives its subjects as anti-Revisionism, the Sino-Soviet split, foreign relations, the Cold War and ideology, its language English (Harvard Digital Handbook). The same record states a limit: "This online resource has not been found to meet all criteria for legitimacy", for it "may reproduce copyright-protected content without license or permissions, contain re-typed content that cannot be verified for accuracy or completeness, and/or omit facts of publication or archival attribution" (Harvard Digital Handbook). The census record states no limits of the saved pages ("not stated on the saved pages"), notes that the gathering method "is not described on the saved page", does not answer "the completeness of its holdings for any organization" or "the record of tendencies outside anti-revisionism", and leaves unchecked "who the EROL Administrator is, and how documents were gathered", its introduction page having returned HTTP 404 (maryleelabor census record). The census asks of it "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", files it under movement documents, an area whose definition includes "the record of splits", and the texts of the tradition, with movement documents, periodical runs and primary texts as its evidence, and answers that it keeps "the anti-revisionist movements, organizations and parties: their primary documents and periodicals, in the encyclopedia's own periodization", which tells "how the encyclopedia periodizes a national movement's waves, splits and collapse" (maryleelabor census record). The archive's reading in the record is "An organ that keeps a defeated tendency's record in that tendency's own documents, sectioned by its splits and its collapse, so each faction of a split stays stated after the organization that housed it ended"; it reads the "Anti-Dogmatists Unable to Unite" and "Major Issues and Debates" sections "as the losing side of the losing side kept for later readers, held by an archive independent of every party it records", and tags it "NOT an organ of any party it records" (maryleelabor census record). The census names #1725, Ils ne sont pas marxistes, as its anchor (maryleelabor census record); #1725 holds that "Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender", and that otherwise "the defeated critique loses its organ, its holder and its route, and so cannot be taken up later" (#1725). #1725 states the conventional reading first, in which "the New Communist Movement's succession of parties" looks like proof and "the left's problem is temperamental: too much fighting", and reads the record by its endings: "Disagreement is constant. What varies is the ending", a critique being "settled by vote, verdict or decree, with the losing position carried into nothing that follows" or leaving "with the people who hold it" (#1725). Where a dispute concerns the group's identity, #1725 holds, "a split is the honest outcome, and the question becomes whether the split is recorded and argued or simply enacted", and where a critique was later taken up its critics "had a base and form of their own, a caucus, collective, journal or paper" (#1725). #1725 draws its SDS case from a document in EROL's New Communist Movement section, the REP collective's account of the 1969 expulsion of Progressive Labor, calls the SDS record "the clearest single instance, because the winning side wrote it down", and concludes "The split took the place of the discussion" (#1725); Challenge/Desafio, the newspaper of the party expelled, stands on the encyclopedia's periodicals page (periodicals page). The English Wikipedia has no article on it: the name redirects to "Marxists Internet Archive", whose article defines the host as "a non-profit online encyclopedia, created in 1990" and names its historical sections and a reference section, the "Encyclopedia of Marxism", without naming EROL (Wikipedia), which the census record tags "NOT a general encyclopedia of Marxism" (maryleelabor census record). At its name the Overview carries the encyclopedia's "Definition, period, countries and periodicals", "Faithful to the encyclopedia's subject and range", with "The MIA named as its host", at a new address, the census name, for an external resource entered in the census the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). The Capture Registry records "THE SPLITS NOT CARRIED", "The composition gives the movement as a country entry", and "its periodization by splits, unity attempts and collapse, is not in the composition", and attributes to #1725 a reading of "EROL as a record kept of a movement's failure to hold its own critiques, organized by that failure" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31); #1725 names omission "the expulsion form: the contested record never reaches the answer-forming context" (#1725).

F11.quote: Historically, in the Communist lexicon, the term “anti-revisionism” has been used to describe opposition to attempts to revise, modify or abandon the fundamentals of revolutionary theory and practice in a manner that was perceived to represent concessions to Communism’s adversaries.
F11.claim: the term's older use: opposition to attempts to revise, modify or abandon revolutionary fundamentals in a manner perceived as concessions to Communism's adversaries

F12.quote: In recent times, however, the term has taken on a more specific meaning. It describes a trend that developed in the pro-Soviet (as opposed to the Trotskyist) Communist movement after World War II.
F12.claim: the term's specific meaning: a trend that developed in the pro-Soviet (as opposed to the Trotskyist) Communist movement after World War II

F13.quote: The growth of this anti-revisionist trend was particularly noticeable at several critical moments in the history of the Communist movement – the shift from WW II-era collaboration between the Soviet Union and the Western Powers to the Cold War, and the crisis inaugurated by the 20th Congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union in 1956.
F13.claim: the trend grew at two critical moments: the shift from wartime collaboration to the Cold War, and the crisis of the CPSU's 20th Congress in 1956

F14.quote: Initially, the anti-revisionists presented a critique of the official Communist Parties “from the left” for having abandoned orthodox Marxism-Leninism (becoming “revisionist,”), and for being insufficiently revolutionary.
F14.claim: the anti-revisionists first criticized the official Communist Parties 'from the left', for abandoning orthodox Marxism-Leninism and for being insufficiently revolutionary

F15.quote: Once the official Communist Parties joined in Khrushchev’s denunciation of Stalin, the defense of Stalin and his legacy became a hallmark of “anti-revisionism.”
F15.claim: after the official parties joined Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin, the defence of Stalin and his legacy became a hallmark of anti-revisionism

F16.quote: Later on, the anti-revisionist movement expanded and diversified to encompass those communists who rejected a pro-Soviet orientation for one aligned either with Chinese or Albanian positions.
F16.claim: the movement later expanded and diversified to encompass communists who rejected a pro-Soviet orientation for one aligned with Chinese or Albanian positions

F17.quote: Anti-revisionism enjoyed its moment of greatest size and influence with numerous “Marxist-Leninist” and “Maoist” parties, groups and publications springing up around the world in the period which began with the Sino-Soviet split of the early 1960s.
F17.claim: its greatest size and influence came with Marxist-Leninist and Maoist parties, groups and publications founded worldwide after the Sino-Soviet split of the early 1960s

F18.quote: Its growth was greatly accelerated by international enthusiasm for the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution in China, but it began to decline in response to controversial Chinese foreign policy decisions in the last years of Mao’s life, his death and the subsequent defeat of the Gang of Four.

Composed from its cards, at their grain or coarser: the definition at the grain of Harvard's catalogue record (B4 F22: 'Digital encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism developed by the Marxists Internet Archive, containing English translations'; F27 'Digital archive'; F23 the MIA as creator), with the contents page's 'PRIMARY DOCUMENTS FROM ANTI-REVISIONIST MOVEMENTS, ORGANIZATIONS AND PARTIES' (B1 F1) as 'primary source documents … and organizational records'; the trend from the definition page (B2 F11–F14, F16–F18) through card 2's snippet, whose words 'Opposition to abandoning orthodox revolutionary theory' T carries and which summarize F11 and are no span of the page; the period 1946 to 1983 (B4 F24, the contents page's sections running 1946-1950 to 1982-1983, F3, F7); the countries (B1 F2, F3, F4, F9; B4 F25), all 26 sections with China and Albania placed among the countries as Harvard's coverage places them; the periodicals (B5 F30–F33: Challenge/Desafio, Workers’ Advocate, The Forge, In Struggle, Proletarian). Available in the field and left out of the composition (§6.2, 'available, not composed'): the encyclopedia's own statement of purpose, 'The goal of the Encyclopedia of Anti-Revisionism is to document this trend', and its signature 'Paul C., 2009' (B2 F20); the New Communist Movement's later sections, 'Birth of the Anti-Dogmatist Trend', 'Crises, Splits and More New Parties', 'Anti-Dogmatists Unable to Unite', 'Collapse and Aftermath', 'Major Issues and Debates' (B1 F5), Canada's 'Crisis and Collapse, 1982-1983' (F7) and Britain's 'High Tide' and 'Ebbing Tide: Decline and Dissolution' (F8), which T composes as 'United States (first to third waves, New Communist Movement)', 'Canada (post-WWII antecedents and waves)' and a bare 'United Kingdom'; the contact 'EROL Administrator' (F10); the entry page's placement in the MIA's History section (B3 F21); the defence of Stalin as the trend's hallmark (B2 F15); the decline after Mao and the turn to an independent left-wing communism (F18's second clause, F19); Harvard's subjects and source types (F26) and its collection (F29); the periodicals named by their splits (B5 F35) and those dated after 1983 (F34). Limit dropped: Harvard's own limit on the card T draws its definition and date from, 'This online resource has not been found to meet all criteria for legitimacy' (B4 F28); T composes the record's attribution and dates and leaves its warning out. Limit dropped also on F11: the older sense is 'opposition to attempts to revise, modify or abandon the fundamentals … in a manner that was perceived to represent concessions to Communism’s adversaries'; T1-2's 'Opposition to abandoning orthodox revolutionary theory' drops 'perceived' and the adversaries clause, and composes the term's historical usage as its definition. Force raised: none observed at the period; T1-3's 'Primarily covers materials spanning roughly 1946 to 1983' hedges Harvard's catalogue date (F24), and the periodicals page, card 5, lists entries dated 1969-93, 2000-2005, 'starting in 2009' and 'begun 2011' (F31, F34), which T leaves out. Substituted reading: T1-2's 'Groups later split to align with either Chinese or Albanian political and ideological positions' composes as a split what the definition page states as expansion, 'expanded and diversified to encompass those communists who rejected a pro-Soviet orientation for one aligned either with Chinese or Albanian positions' (F16); T1-3's 'growing significantly during the Sino-Soviet split and the Chinese Cultural Revolution' attaches to the collection's materials the growth the definition page states of the trend (F17, F18). T1-2 drops F12's 'pro-Soviet (as opposed to the Trotskyist)', which card 2's snippet carries ('pro-Soviet'). Composed without attribution: the definition of the trend, at the definition page's grain, with markers and no name; coarse, common-knowledge grain, recorded. The operator attribution 'developed by the Marxists Internet Archive' is Harvard's (F22), carried as a fact with markers. Outside the cards: 'party histories', 'foundational essays', 'regional documents' (no field claim states them); 'translations' is Harvard's 'English translations' (F22). Not surfaced, admitted to B by the operator's ruling: the host's introduction (B6: an 'all-volunteer, non-profit public library', politically independent, endorsing no writer's views, its material 'public domain' unless noted, F36–F41) and Wikipedia (B8: the name a redirect to the host's article, which does not name the encyclopedia, F42–F45). Of the cards' 35 claims, T composes 21 at their grain or coarser.
delta.T_vs_LB_reading: v0.9 §0.5: the first diff is ontological and narrow. T and the field agree on the entity (an online encyclopedia of anti-revisionist documents, hosted by the MIA). T composes the encyclopedia as a catalogue entry would, at Harvard's grain: host, translations, period, countries, periodicals. It leaves out what the encyclopedia's own pages say of its organization and purpose: the sections titled by the movements' splits and collapse, the signed statement of its goal, the administrator; and it leaves out the limit Harvard sets beside the description it takes. Its period is the catalogue's, and its 'split' is its own word for the trend's expansion.
delta.LB_vs_LBA: Admission adds, in one claim space with the field's: the census's question and its answer, field by field (ML-01–ML-36): whose record it keeps (ML-10), who holds it and on what terms (ML-04, ML-11, ML-32), its losing side as its structure, 'organized around splits and defeat' (ML-12, ML-13), the tendency itself 'a minority defined against 'revisionism'' (ML-14), and the archive's reading of it as 'An organ that keeps a defeated tendency's record' and of two of its sections as 'the losing side of the losing side' (ML-24, ML-25), with what the record leaves open (ML-15, ML-20, ML-22, ML-23, ML-33, ML-34); the anchor's account of how disputes end and what keeps a defeated critique (#1725: O1725-01–O1725-07), its SDS case drawn from a document EROL holds, read as the winning side's record (D1725-01, D1725-02), set beside the expelled party's newspaper on the periodicals page (F31); and the Capture Registry's account of the composition at the name (CAP-1-01–CAP-1-12), with #1725's naming of omission as 'the expulsion form' (O1725-08). Held under P_coh within the one ontology: the census's period ('to the 1980s', ML-17), lifecycle (ML-28) and tag 'NOT a living movement's site' (ML-31) beside the periodicals dated 2000-2011 (F34); the census's licence (ML-27) beside Harvard's limit (F28) and Wikipedia's 'not necessarily free of copyright' (F44); the census's reading of the encyclopedia as keeping the defeated tendency's own documents (ML-24) beside #1725's use of it for the winning side's account (D1725-01). Not surfaced: every archive source; no card cites the census record (CAP-1-12: the record entered the census the same day).

loci.quote: online encyclopedia of information on, and primary documents from, anti-revisionist movements, organizations and parties, by country

An organ that keeps a defeated tendency's record in that tendency's own documents, sectioned by its splits and its collapse, so each faction of a split stays stated after the organization that housed it ended.
Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?

Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender.

And it cannot be avoided where the dispute concerns the group's identity, because there a split is the honest outcome, and the question becomes whether the split is recorded and argued or simply enacted.
The **SDS** record is the clearest single instance, because the winning side wrote it down. … ([REP collective](https://www.marxists.org/history/erol/ncm-1/rep-sds.pdf))
The feature that makes EROL a record of the left's internal history, its periodization by splits, unity attempts and collapse, is not in the composition.
